title: Data & Methods
text:
How I Loaded the Data
I created a MySQL database on Amazon RDS and named the schema FAA.
First, I used the provided CreateFactTable.sql file to create the al_perf table. Then, I used an EC2 instance and mysqlimport to load the flight CSV into the database.
I imported the lookup tables through MySQL Workbench. I then ran SQL queries in MySQL Workbench and exported the results as CSV files.
The import reported 590,581 records, with no skipped or deleted records. It also reported 58,597 warnings. These warnings made me check the imported data more closely.

title: Data & Methods
text:
What I Checked

Row Count and Dates
I used SQL to count the records in al_perf and check their dates.
The table contained 590,581 records, which matched the number reported by the import tool. All records were from December 2024. The earliest date was December 1, and the latest was December 31.


Departure Delay Values
I used SQL to count NULL, zero, negative, and positive values in the DepDelay column.

Cancelled Flights and Zero Delays
I also grouped the records by cancellation status and counted how many flights had a departure delay of zero.

Many cancelled flights had a departure delay of zero. This made me question whether every zero meant an on-time departure.
Because the import produced warnings, I suspected that some missing values might have become zeros during import. However, my SQL checks alone could not confirm this explanation or show how many values might have been affected.
I kept the stored values unchanged. I did not replace all zeros with NULL because zero can also be a valid departure delay.

title: Data & Methods
text:
How I Defined the Analysis
I used the following rules in my SQL queries.







Question
What I calculated




Q1
The largest departure delay for each airline, sorted from smallest to largest.


Q2
The greatest number of minutes early for each airline, with airline names listed from largest to smallest early departure.


Q3
The number of non-cancelled flights for each weekday, ranked from busiest to least busy.


Q4
The airport with the highest average departure delay, using non-cancelled flights and treating early departures as zero delay.


Q5
For each airline, the airport with its highest average departure delay, using the same rules as Q4.


Q6
The number of cancelled flights and the most common cancellation reason at each departure airport.


Q7
The average daily flight count over the current day and the previous two days, using non-cancelled flights.



For Q1 and Q2, I used the departure delay values stored in the database. Q2 only considered negative departure delays.
For Q3–Q5 and Q7, I chose to exclude cancelled flights. This keeps the flight counts and delay comparisons focused on non-cancelled flights.
For Q4, the question requires early departures to count as zero delay. For Q5, I chose to use the same rule so that the two average-delay analyses use a consistent definition.
These choices are part of my analysis and are stated here to make the results easier to understand.

How I Handled Ties
For Q3, weekdays with the same flight count receive the same rank. The next rank may skip a number.
For Q4, the query returns one airport. If average delays tie, airport code determines which airport is selected.
For Q5, the query returns one airport per airline. If two airports share the highest average delay, airport code determines which one is selected.
For Q6, I keep all cancellation reasons tied for the highest count at an airport. Therefore, an airport may appear more than once in the results.


How the Three-Day Average Works
For Q7, I first counted non-cancelled flights for each date. Then I calculated a moving average.
For example, the December 3 average uses the flight counts from December 1, 2, and 3.
The beginning of the month has fewer available days:

December 1 uses only December 1.
December 2 uses December 1 and 2.
December 3 onward uses the current day and the previous two days.

The daily query results include all 31 days of December, so each three-row window represents three consecutive dates.

title: Data & Methods
text:
Things to Keep in Mind

The results describe December 2024 in this dataset. Other months may show different patterns.
A maximum delay describes an extreme event, not an airline’s usual performance.
An airport with only a few flights can have a high average because of one or two long delays.
Some weekdays occur more often than others in December. This affects total flight counts by weekday.
A non-cancelled flight may still have been diverted.
The import warnings were not fully investigated. The SQL checks describe the stored data, but they do not prove that every source value was preserved correctly during import.

This project examines U.S. flight performance in December 2024, focusing on departure delays, early departures, flight activity, and cancellations.
The analysis uses SQL to summarize flight records and combines the results with visualizations to explain patterns across airlines, airports, and dates.

title: Conclusions
text:
Hagerstown (HGR) had the highest average departure delay in Q4, at 107.38 minutes.
Sunday had the most non-cancelled flights, while Wednesday had the fewest. These are monthly totals.
There were 4,151 cancelled flights. Weather was the leading cancellation reason in all ten airport–reason results shown.
Daily flight counts dropped on December 24–25 and increased again on December 26.

title: Conclusions
text:
Limitations
These results cover only December 2024. Maximum delays describe extreme events, and airport averages should be considered alongside flight counts.
The import produced warnings. My SQL checks raised questions about zero departure delays among cancelled flights, but did not confirm whether missing values were converted to zeros.

title: Conclusions
text:
What I Learned
This project gave me practice loading data into MySQL, joining lookup tables, and using grouping and window functions. I also used Python to turn my exported SQL results into charts for this Quarto report.
